title: How Junk Food Works
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore junk food: its definition as high-calorie, low-nutrient "empty calorie" food, and its history from early caramels and chocolate through the industrialization of food, the Civil War ration era, the rise of fast food and diners, and early snack brands like Cracker Jack, Tootsie Roll, Popsicle, potato chips, Big Gulp, Clark Bar, Pop-Tarts, and Double Stuf/Oreo versus Hydrox. They cover the food science of "bliss point," mouth feel, vanishing caloric density (Cheetos), flavor layering (Doritos), and line extensions, plus the Lunchables story and marketing to children. Health effects discussed include obesity, heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and addiction-like behavior. The episode closes with Michael Moss's New York Times article on addictive junk food, a Kansas State nutrition professor's ten-week junk food diet experiment, and a listener correction about the term "Aborigines."
topics: Michael Moss New York Times article

segments.title: Opening banter and junk food definition
segments.summary: Hosts reference past episodes on related topics, then define junk food as food with little nutritional value and many calories, often carbs, leading to stored fat, and note possible links to mental and physical health.

segments.title: Pre-junk food diets and industrialization
segments.summary: Discussion of how past generations ate mostly what they grew or harvested, and how the Industrial Revolution and cheap flour made processed food possible. Early sweets like caramels and chocolate are mentioned, along with Keebler's early bakery.

segments.title: Canning and tangents
segments.summary: The hosts digress into home canning, Chuck's memories of a county cannery, and a tangent about boring places for kids such as tire stores and fabric stores.

segments.title: Fast food, Civil War rations, and diners
segments.summary: Fast food is distinguished from junk food, with Chipotle and McDonald's mentioned. The hosts say Civil War troops developed a taste for canned rations, and that food carts parked outside factories evolved into diners.

segments.title: Early American junk food origin stories
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the origins of Cracker Jack, Tootsie Roll, Popsicle (Frank Epperson), potato chips, and the early soda and Big Gulp history.

segments.title: Candy bars, Pop-Tarts, Oreo and Hydrox, gum
segments.summary: Brief mentions of the Clark Bar, Pop-Tarts' earlier name, the Hydrox and Oreo rivalry, and the Double Bubble gum inventor.

segments.title: Bliss point, mouth feel, and vanishing caloric density
segments.summary: Food companies research the bliss point and mouth feel. Cheetos are described as melting quickly so the brain does not register calories, and fat's greasy feel is discussed. Soda is described as balancing greasy fast food.

segments.title: Childhood broccoli and milk anecdote
segments.summary: Chuck tells a personal story about hating broccoli and milk as a child, and the hosts discuss drinking soda or water with fast food.

segments.title: Health effects: obesity, addiction, type 2 diabetes
segments.summary: Risks of junk food are reviewed: obesity, heart disease, type 2 diabetes, depression, and addiction-like patterns. Americans' average sugar intake and how repeated blood sugar spikes wear out insulin-producing cells are explained, along with diabetic foot complications and pre-diabetes.

segments.title: Documentaries on food: Fed Up, Super Size Me, Super High Me
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the documentary Fed Up narrated by Katie Couric and discuss Super Size Me and Super High Me.

segments.title: Michael Moss article and Lunchables
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Michael Moss's New York Times article on addictive junk food, the food industry's resistance to healthier products, and the Lunchables story: its development with Oscar Meyer and Kraft, use of cheese food, and marketing to children at child eye level.
topics: Michael Moss New York Times article

segments.title: Junk food diet experiment
segments.summary: A Kansas State University nutrition professor, Mark Haub, ate a junk food diet for ten weeks at reduced calories; he lost weight and his cholesterol profile improved. The hosts discuss that calories matter more than their source and that the long-term effects are unknown.

segments.title: Listener mail: Aborigines terminology
segments.summary: A listener named Krista corrects the hosts' earlier use of the term Aborigines and notes that puberty rituals were practiced by some groups, not all. The hosts thank her.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts ask listeners to reach out via Twitter, Facebook, email, or the website, and sign off.
